title: Permutations of Strings
directAnswer: Generate **all permutations of a string in lexicographic (dictionary) order**. Sort the characters first, then backtrack with a `used[]` array: at each position loop the sorted characters left to right, skip used ones, and — to handle repeated letters — skip a duplicate character when its identical predecessor hasn't been used at this level. Choosing in sorted order with that dedup rule emits permutations already sorted, so no final sort is needed. There are up to n! permutations, so the cost is O(n · n!).

remember.pattern: Sort + backtracking with used[] and same-level duplicate skip (lexicographic emission)
remember.formula:
chars = sorted(s)

def backtrack(path):
    if len(path) == n: emit(''.join(path)); return
    for i in range(n):
        if used[i]: continue
        if i > 0 and chars[i] == chars[i-1] and not used[i-1]: continue  # dedup
        used[i] = True; path.append(chars[i])
        backtrack(path)
        path.pop(); used[i] = False
rules: **Sort the characters first** — iterating them in order is what makes the output lexicographic without a post-sort.
Use a `used[]` array (no start index) so every position can draw any not-yet-placed character — order matters in permutations.
Dedup repeated letters with `if chars[i] == chars[i-1] and not used[i-1]: continue` — skips identical siblings at the same level so each distinct permutation appears once.
Restore **both** `path.pop()` and `used[i] = False` on backtrack — asymmetric undo is the classic bug.
Emit a **copy/join** at a full-length leaf only; partial paths aren't permutations.
whenToUse: All arrangements of a string/array, especially required in sorted order
Lexicographic enumeration where a stream of permutations is consumed in order
Input may contain repeated characters and duplicates must be collapsed
Anagram listing, password/keyspace enumeration of small length
antiSignals: Only the NEXT permutation is needed → use next_permutation (O(n)), not full enumeration
Only the COUNT of distinct permutations → it's n! / (product of duplicate factorials), no enumeration
All characters distinct and order of output irrelevant → plain permutations, skip sort + dedup
n is large (> ~10) → n! is infeasible to enumerate
remember.takeaway: Lexicographic string permutations = sort the characters so the backtracking visits them in order, then apply the standard used[] permutation template with one extra line — the same-level duplicate skip. Master the dedup rule here and Permutations II, Subsets II, and Combination Sum II reuse it verbatim.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you produce permutations in lexicographic order by sorting first (not by sorting the result afterwards), use the used[] template correctly, and handle repeated characters with the same-level skip.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Generating all permutations then sorting (works but signals you didn't see the cleaner emission), forgetting the duplicate-skip so repeated letters produce duplicate permutations, or omitting `used[i] = false` on backtrack.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain why iterating sorted characters yields lexicographic output directly, articulate the `chars[i]==chars[i-1] && !used[i-1]` dedup precisely, and note that for just the next permutation you'd switch to the O(n) next_permutation algorithm.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, generate **all permutations** of its characters and return them in **lexicographically sorted (dictionary) order**.

If the string contains repeated characters, each *distinct* permutation must appear exactly once.

For example, `s = "ab"` returns `["ab", "ba"]`, and `s = "aba"` returns `["aab", "aba", "baa"]`.
constraints: s consists of printable characters (commonly lowercase letters)
The string may contain repeated characters
Output must be in lexicographic order with no duplicate permutations
Number of distinct permutations ≤ n! (fewer when characters repeat)
understanding: Produce every distinct ordering of the characters, sorted as a dictionary would. Because permutations care about order, there's no start index — every position can take any unused character. Sorting the characters up front means the backtracking explores them smallest-first, so results come out already sorted. Repeated characters would otherwise yield duplicate permutations; a same-level skip collapses them so each distinct arrangement is emitted once.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should the output be sorted, or is any order acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lexicographically sorted. We achieve that by sorting the characters first and iterating them in order — no need to sort the final list.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the string contain duplicate characters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. We must emit each distinct permutation once, so a same-level duplicate skip (`chars[i]==chars[i-1] && !used[i-1]`) is required.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does every permutation use all characters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a permutation is a full rearrangement, so each result has length n. We record only at full-length leaves.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the string get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to length 10, so at most 10! = 3,628,800 permutations — large but enumerable. The small bound confirms full enumeration is intended.

approaches.complexityReasoning: Generating permutations is O(n · n!). Deduping via a set is O(n) per permutation. The final sort of up to n! strings of length n costs O(n · n! · log(n!)). Storage holds all permutations → O(n · n!).
approaches.explanation:
The most direct route: enumerate first, tidy up after.

**Enumerate.** Run the textbook permutation backtracking — `used[]` array, choose/explore/un-choose, record at full length — without worrying about order or repeats. This yields all n! orderings (with duplicates if characters repeat).

**Dedup.** Insert each permutation into a `set` so identical strings (from swapping two equal characters) collapse to one.

**Sort.** The set is unordered, so sort the distinct permutations lexicographically before returning.

**Why it's only a baseline.** It's correct and easy to reason about, but it pays twice: it generates duplicate work for repeated characters (then throws it away), and it sorts n! strings at the end. The optimal version sorts the *characters once* up front so the search emits permutations already distinct and already sorted — turning an O(n·n!·log n!) finish into linear collection. Lead with this to show you can get a correct answer, then refine.
approaches.insight: Sorting the output is the lazy way to get lexicographic order; sorting the input is the smart way. Whenever 'sorted results' is required from an enumeration, ask whether ordering the choices up front removes the post-sort entirely.

approaches.name: Sort + Backtracking with Duplicate Skip (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The clean answer. Phrase it as 'sort the characters so the search visits them in order, then skip same-level duplicates'.
hints: Sort the characters first. Iterating them smallest-first at every position makes the permutations come out in lexicographic order with no post-sort.
Use a `used[]` array (no start index — order matters). At each level loop i from 0, skip used[i].

To avoid duplicate permutations from repeated characters, skip a character equal to its predecessor when that predecessor isn't currently used: `chars[i]==chars[i-1] && !used[i-1] → continue`. Record at a full-length leaf.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n), dominated by the enumeration. There are at most n! distinct permutations, each costing O(n) to build/emit → O(n · n!). Extra space is the recursion depth (n), the path (n), and used[] (n) → O(n) beyond the output.
approaches.explanation:
Two ideas combine: emit in order, and emit each distinct permutation once.

**Sort so output is sorted.** Sort the characters before searching. At every position we loop the characters from index 0 upward, so we always try the smallest available character first. Doing that at every level means the very first complete permutation is the smallest, the next is the next-smallest, and so on — the results stream out in dictionary order. No final sort is needed.

**used[] because order matters.** Permutations are an 'order matters' problem, so there is no start index: position 0 can be any character, position 1 any of the rest. A boolean `used[]` tracks which characters are already in the current path; we `continue` past used ones so each character appears once per permutation.

**The duplicate-skip line.** With repeated characters, two identical letters at different indices would generate the same permutation twice. The fix is one line: `if (i > 0 && chars[i] == chars[i-1] && !used[i-1]) continue;`. Read it as: *don't start a branch with this character if an identical character just before it is still available and unused at this level.* That forces equal characters to be consumed in their fixed left-to-right order, so each distinct arrangement is produced exactly once. The `!used[i-1]` part is crucial — if the predecessor *is* used (it's part of the current path), then this `chars[i]` is a legitimately different position to fill, not a duplicate sibling.

**Symmetric undo.** Choosing does `used[i] = true` and `path.append`; un-choosing must undo both with `path.pop()` and `used[i] = false`. Forget the second and the character stays marked forever, dropping permutations.

**Record at full length.** A permutation uses all n characters, so we snapshot the path only when `len(path) == n`.
approaches.insight: Lexicographic order is bought by sorting the *choices*, not the *results*. And the one-line same-level duplicate skip — 'skip an equal sibling whose twin is still unused' — is the single most reused trick across Permutations II, Subsets II, and Combination Sum II. Learn it once, apply it everywhere duplicates must collapse.

code.python:
def permutations(s: str) -> list[str]:
    chars = sorted(s)                          # sort → lexicographic emission
    n = len(chars)
    used = [False] * n
    results: list[str] = []
    path: list[str] = []

    def backtrack() -> None:
        if len(path) == n:
            results.append(''.join(path))      # full-length leaf → record
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if used[i]:
                continue                       # already placed
            if i > 0 and chars[i] == chars[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]:
                continue                       # skip duplicate sibling
            used[i] = True                     # choose
            path.append(chars[i])
            backtrack()                        # explore
            path.pop()                         # un-choose: restore BOTH
            used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return results

java.explanation: Sorting the characters makes the in-order traversal produce sorted permutations directly.
A permutation uses all characters; record only at full length.
Skip an equal sibling whose identical predecessor is still unused — collapses duplicate permutations.
Mark the character placed so deeper levels skip it.
Pop the character; the next line unmarks it — both must be undone.

The dedup skip blocks the second branch → only ["aa"], not ["aa", "aa"].

pitfalls: Sorting the result instead of the input — works but wastes an O(n·n!·log n!) sort.
Dropping the `!used[i-1]` condition in the dedup — over-skips and loses valid permutations.
Forgetting `used[i] = false` on backtrack — leaves characters marked and loses permutations.

commonMistakes: Generating all permutations and sorting afterwards instead of sorting the characters first.
Omitting the same-level duplicate skip, so repeated characters yield duplicate permutations.
Forgetting to reset `used[i] = false` after recursion, dropping most permutations.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing duplicate skip
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With repeated characters, two identical letters generate the same permutation twice. The same-level skip collapses them so each distinct permutation appears once.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting the output, not the input
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Sorting n! results at the end is far costlier than sorting the n characters once. Iterating sorted characters emits permutations already in order.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Asymmetric backtrack
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Choosing sets used[i] = true and appends; if un-choose only pops, the character stays marked for every sibling branch and most permutations vanish.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
used[i] = True; path.append(chars[i])
backtrack()
path.pop()                # used[i] never reset!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
used[i] = True; path.append(chars[i])
backtrack()
path.pop(); used[i] = False   # restore BOTH
